original_value: The emerging Internet of Things has the potential to solve major societal challenges associated with healthcare provision. Low-power wireless protocols for residential Health Internet of Things applications are characterized by high reliability requirements, the need for energy-efficient operation, and the need to operate robustly in diverse environments in the presence of external interference. We enhance and experimentally evaluate the Time-Slotted Channel Hopping protocol from the IEEE 802.15.4 standard to address these challenges. Our contributions are a new schedule and an adaptive channel selection mechanism to increase the performance of time-slotted channel hopping in this domain. Evaluation in a test house shows that the enhanced system is suitable for our e-Health application and compares favorably with state-of-the-art options. The schedule provides higher reliability compared with the minimal scheduling function from the IETF 6TiSCH Working Group and has a better energy-efficiency/reliability tradeoff than the Orchestra scheduler. Results from 29 long-term residential deployments confirm the suitability for the application and show that the system is able to adapt and avoid channels used by WiFi. In these uncontrolled environments, the system achieves 99.96% average reliability for networks that generate 7.5 packets per second on average.

result.paraphrase: The rise of the Internet of Things could help address major healthcare delivery challenges. Residential Health Internet of Things applications using low-power wireless protocols demand very high reliability, energy-efficient operation, and robust performance across varied environments despite external interference. To meet these needs, we improve and experimentally assess the IEEE 802.15.4 Time-Slotted Channel Hopping protocol. Our work introduces a new schedule and an adaptive channel-selection mechanism to boost time-slotted channel hopping performance in this setting. Tests in a house demonstrate that the enhanced system is appropriate for our e-Health application and performs favorably against state-of-the-art alternatives. The schedule is more reliable than the IETF 6TiSCH Working Group’s minimal scheduling function and offers a better energy-efficiency/reliability balance than the Orchestra scheduler. Findings from 29 long-term residential deployments further confirm the system’s suitability and show that it can adapt to and avoid WiFi-used channels. In these uncontrolled environments, the system reaches 99.96% average reliability for networks generating 7.5 packets per second on average.
